title: Multidimensional Frailty-Related Vulnerability Profiles Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults: A Data-Driven Cluster Analysis of the 2023 National Survey of Older Koreans
content: Background/Objectives: Frailty-related vulnerability spans health, physical function, health behaviors, cognition, and psychological well-being. A single summary score may not fully convey how these features co-occur within individuals. This study identified data-driven frailty-related profiles among community-dwelling older adults and compared the magnitude of between-profile differences. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional secondary analysis of the 2023 National Survey of Older Koreans. The analytical sample included 9,950 participants. Ten indicators—self-rated health, chronic disease count, 1-year weight loss, sleep quality, weekly exercise frequency, fatigue, stair-climbing ability, 300-m walking ability, cognitive function, and depressive symptoms—were standardized and entered into K-means clustering. Candidate solutions for K = 2–10 were evaluated using within-cluster sums of squares and mean silhouette coefficients. Profile characteristics and effect sizes were compared using independent-samples t-tests, Pearson’s chi-squared tests, Cohen’s d, and Cramér’s V. Results: The K = 2 solution had the highest mean silhouette coefficient (0.273). Within the analytic sample, 6,962 participants (70.0%) formed a lower-vulnerability profile and 2,988 (30.0%) a multidimensional higher-vulnerability profile. The latter profile showed less favorable health, functional, psychological, and cognitive characteristics. The largest between-profile differences occurred in 300 m unassisted walking (d = 2.013) and climbing 10 stairs without assistance (d = 2.001), followed by self-rated health (d = 1.582), and depressive symptoms (d = 1.418). Conclusions: The two profiles reflected relative multidimensional vulnerability differences within the analytical sample rather than predefined clinical frailty categories. Multidimensional assessments may provide complementary information for older adult healthcare, although external and longitudinal validation is needed before broader clinical application.
